deepDive.heading: What Does a Full Rewire Actually Involve?

Glasgow's tenement and period flats bring their own quirks that a generic rewire quote won't account for — lath-and-plaster walls behave differently to modern stud walls when it comes to chasing cable routes, and shared stairwells or factor-managed common areas sometimes need a quick word with the factor before we touch anything communal. We've worked enough of these properties across the city to know which questions to ask before we start, not halfway through.

deepDive.heading: What We Actually Test During an EICR
paragraphs: An EICR isn't a quick visual once-over — it's a full inspection combining a visual check of accessible wiring and fittings with 'dead testing' (checked with the power off, covering continuity, insulation resistance, and earthing) and 'live testing' (checked with the power on, covering RCD trip times and polarity).

Every issue we find gets a code, not just a pass/fail: C1 means danger present, needing action immediately; C2 means potentially dangerous, needing to be addressed urgently; C3 is an improvement recommended but not a compliance failure; and FI means further investigation is needed. We explain what each one actually means for your property in plain English on the day, not just in a report you get later.

deepDive.heading: RCDs, RCBOs, and Why Your Board Actually Matters
paragraphs: An old rewireable fuse box protects your wiring from overheating — that's it. It does nothing to protect a person from electric shock, because it has no RCD (residual current device) protection, which is why boards like these are one of the most common issues we flag on an EICR.

A modern consumer unit fits RCDs or RCBOs (a combined breaker and RCD per circuit) as standard, which cut the power in milliseconds if they detect current leaking somewhere it shouldn't — like through a person. We size and split circuits properly across the board so one nuisance trip doesn't take out your whole house, which is the other common complaint we hear about old or badly-specified boards.

concerns.q: Do I need a whole new board, or can mine be repaired?
concerns.a: If it's an old rewireable fuse box with no RCD protection, repairing it isn't really an option — it needs replacing to meet current safety standards. If it's a modern board with one faulty part, sometimes a repair genuinely is enough, and we'll tell you honestly which applies.

concerns.q: Is my current board safe to keep using in the meantime?

Second fix comes after plastering and decoration — we come back to actually terminate everything: fitting sockets, switches, light fittings, and connecting into the consumer unit. faqs.a: There's no single law naming PAT testing directly, but the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require equipment to be maintained safely — PAT testing is the standard, recognised way to demonstrate that. Many insurers and letting agents treat it as effectively mandatory.

deepDive.heading: What Actually Gets Checked During PAT Testing
paragraphs: PAT testing is two steps, not one: a visual inspection of the plug, cable, and casing for obvious damage, followed by an electrical test of earth continuity, insulation resistance, and — where relevant — polarity. Most failures are caught at the visual stage, before the equipment is even plugged into a tester.

Every item gets a pass or fail label with the date, so it's obvious at a glance what's current and what's due. We keep a digital register alongside the physical labels, so if a certificate ever needs to be produced for an insurer, letting agent, or auditor, it's a five-minute job to pull it up rather than a search through a filing cabinet.

faqs.q: What does the Scottish interlinked alarm standard actually require?
faqs.a: Broadly: one smoke alarm in the room most used during the day, one in every circulation space like hallways and landings, a heat alarm in the kitchen, and a carbon monoxide alarm anywhere there's a fuel-burning appliance — all interlinked, so if one goes off, they all do.

faqs.q: Is this a legal requirement or just a recommendation?
faqs.a: It's a legal requirement for all homes in Scotland, regardless of tenure — owner-occupied, rented, or social housing.

faqs.q: Can you fit this alongside other electrical work?
faqs.a: Yes, it's often most efficient to have interlinked alarms wired in as part of a rewire or consumer unit upgrade — ask us to include it when you get a quote for other work.

faqs.q: How long does installation take?
faqs.a: A straightforward retrofit in an average home is usually completed within a day.

benefit: Interlinked Alarms, Fitted to the Scottish Standard

deepDive.heading: Getting the Interlinked Alarm Standard Right
paragraphs: The most common mistake we find isn't a missing alarm — it's alarms that exist but aren't actually interlinked, or a heat alarm in the kitchen that's been swapped for a smoke alarm at some point, which isn't compliant. We start every job by checking what's already there against the standard, not assuming a full new system is needed.

Where mains wiring back to the consumer unit is straightforward, that's usually the best long-term option. In tenement flats or properties where chasing cable routes would mean significant disruption, a wireless-interlinked system using long-life alarms meets the same standard with far less work — we'll be upfront about which makes sense for your property before quoting.

concerns.q: Will this involve chasing walls or major disruption?
concerns.a: Only if you specifically want full mains wiring — wireless-interlinked alarms are a genuine, compliant alternative with minimal disruption.

concerns.q: Do I need this if I'm not selling or renting?
concerns.a: Yes, the standard applies to all homes in Scotland regardless of whether you're selling, letting, or simply living in the property.

faqs.q: Why does my circuit keep tripping?
faqs.a: It's usually one of a few things: a faulty appliance, damaged cable, a failing RCD, or a circuit that's simply overloaded. We isolate which one it is systematically rather than replacing parts until it stops.

faqs.q: Is a tripping circuit an emergency?
faqs.a: Not always, but it shouldn't be ignored — repeated tripping is often an early warning sign. If it's happening frequently or you can smell burning, treat it as urgent and get in touch straight away.

faqs.q: How quickly can you get to a fault?
faqs.a: We aim for same-day response on genuine faults. Call rather than email if it's urgent — it's the fastest way to get a time confirmed.

faqs.q: Will you know what's wrong before you arrive?
faqs.a: Sometimes we can narrow it down over the phone, but most faults need an on-site diagnosis to trace properly — we don't guess and hope.

faqs.q: Do you fix the fault on the same visit?
faqs.a: In most cases yes, once it's diagnosed. If parts need ordering or it turns out to be a bigger job, we'll explain that clearly and quote before doing anything further.

benefit: The Actual Cause Found, Not Just the Nearest Symptom

deepDive.heading: How We Actually Trace an Electrical Fault
paragraphs: Fault finding starts with questions, not tools — when it happens, what's plugged in at the time, whether it's one circuit or several. That narrows things down before we even open the consumer unit. From there we isolate circuits one at a time, testing insulation resistance and continuity to find exactly where the fault is, rather than replacing the first suspicious-looking component.

The reason this matters is that a quick fix aimed at the wrong cause just brings the customer back a few weeks later with the same trip. We'd rather spend the extra twenty minutes tracing it properly and fix it once.

concerns.q: What if you can't find the fault straight away?
concerns.a: Intermittent faults can take longer to isolate — we'll be honest if a job needs a second visit rather than pushing through and guessing.

concerns.q: Will I be without power while you work?
concerns.a: Only the affected circuit is usually isolated, not the whole property, and we'll tell you what to expect before starting.

deepDive.heading: Why We Check Circuit Load Before Adding a Socket
paragraphs: Adding a socket looks simple from the outside, but the question that actually matters is what's already running on that circuit — a ring main with several heavy appliances already on it behaves differently to a lightly loaded circuit in a spare room. faqs.q: Is an extractor fan a legal requirement in bathrooms?
faqs.a: Building Regulations Part F requires adequate ventilation in bathrooms and kitchens, particularly where there's no openable window — a correctly specified extractor fan is the standard way to meet this.

faqs.q: Where should extractor fan ducting actually go?
faqs.a: Out to the external air, ideally by the shortest practical route — venting into a loft space instead is a common shortcut that just moves the damp problem rather than solving it.

faqs.q: What's the difference between timer and humidity-sensing fans?
faqs.a: A timer runs for a set period after the light's switched on; a humidity sensor detects moisture in the air and runs automatically regardless of the light switch — useful for baths or showers left running without the light on.

faqs.q: Can a fan be wired to run with the light?

faqs.q: How noisy should a new fan be?

deepDive.heading: Why Ducting Route Matters More Than the Fan Itself
paragraphs: The fan unit gets most of the attention, but the ducting route is what actually determines whether extraction works. A fan venting into a loft space rather than outside just relocates the moisture problem, which is exactly what we find on a lot of older installations we're called out to fix.

Zoning matters just as much in a bathroom — fans and their switching need to be positioned and rated correctly for the wet zones they're near. We plan this properly as standard, along with humidity sensing or timer overrun depending on how the room's actually used, rather than fitting a generic fan and switch combination.

concerns.q: Can you fix a fan that's already installed but not working properly?

benefit: Power That Matches What Your Equipment Actually Needs

deepDive.heading: Getting the Load Calculation Right Before Any Work Starts
paragraphs: The single biggest mistake we see with three-phase work is sizing the supply or distribution board to what's needed today, with no allowance for what a business will actually run in two or three years. We calculate load based on your current equipment list and reasonable near-term expansion, not just what's plugged in on the day we visit.

Where an upgraded supply from the network operator is required, that process has its own timeline outside our control — we'll be upfront about this early, rather than leaving it as a surprise partway through a project, so it can be factored into your own planning and any equipment delivery dates.

faqs.q: How much can LED high-bay lighting actually save on running costs?
faqs.a: It varies by site and current fittings, but replacing older fluorescent or sodium high-bay lighting with LED commonly cuts lighting energy use significantly, on top of far longer fitting lifespan and less maintenance.

faqs.q: How do you work out how many fittings a warehouse needs?

benefit: Even Coverage, Lower Running Costs, Less Maintenance

deepDive.heading: Why Fitting Count Alone Doesn't Determine Good Coverage
paragraphs: A common mistake with high-bay lighting upgrades is simply matching the number of existing fittings with new LED equivalents, without recalculating for the actual output and spread of the new fittings. LEDs distribute light differently to older fluorescent or sodium fittings, so a like-for-like fitting count can genuinely leave a warehouse under- or unevenly lit even after an upgrade.

We calculate layouts from ceiling height, floor area, and the lux level appropriate to how each zone is actually used — a picking aisle and a loading bay don't need identical lighting, and treating them the same either overspends on fittings or leaves working areas under-lit.

concerns.q: Will the warehouse need to shut down during the upgrade?
concerns.a: Not usually — phased or zoned upgrade work can often be carried out around ongoing operations, and we'll plan this with you specifically for your site.

concerns.q: Do LED high-bay fittings need much maintenance?
concerns.a: Considerably less than fluorescent or sodium fittings — longer fitting lifespan is one of the main practical benefits alongside the energy savings.

faqs.q: What's load management and why does it matter for fleet charging?
faqs.a: Load management dynamically balances power across multiple charge points so they can all operate without exceeding your site's supply capacity — without it, charging several vehicles at once can trip your supply or require a costly capacity upgrade you may not actually need.

faqs.q: How many charge points can our current supply handle?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on your existing supply capacity and other site loads — we assess this properly before recommending a specific number of points or whether a supply upgrade makes sense.

faqs.q: Is forklift charging different to EV vehicle charging?
faqs.a: The underlying electrical principles are similar, but forklift charging stations and layouts have their own practical considerations around warehouse floor space and usage patterns, which we plan for specifically.

faqs.q: Can charging infrastructure be installed in phases as our fleet grows?
faqs.a: Yes, this is a common and sensible approach — we can design the initial installation with future expansion in mind, rather than needing to redo groundwork later.

faqs.q: Do you handle the electrical side only, or the full charge point setup?
faqs.a: We handle the full electrical installation including the charge points themselves, load management, and supply assessment — a complete, tested, certified installation.

benefit: Charging Infrastructure Sized for Fleet Use, Not Retrofitted

deepDive.heading: Why Load Management Matters More As Fleets Grow
paragraphs: A single EV charger is a relatively simple electrical addition. Multiple charge points serving a fleet is a different problem entirely — if every point could theoretically draw maximum power simultaneously, the supply capacity required becomes expensive fast. Load management solves this by dynamically sharing available capacity across active charge points, so a smaller supply can still serve more vehicles than a naive calculation would suggest.

We design fleet and forklift charging installations around your actual usage pattern — how many vehicles charge overnight versus during shift changes, for example — rather than assuming worst-case simultaneous demand across every point, which usually leads to over-specifying (and overpaying for) supply capacity you'll rarely actually need.

concerns.q: What if we need to add more charge points later than planned?
concerns.a: We can design the initial supply and infrastructure with reasonable headroom for expansion, so adding points later doesn't necessarily mean redoing the groundwork.

concerns.q: Will this require a supply upgrade from our energy provider?
concerns.a: Sometimes, depending on your fleet size and existing capacity — we'll assess this honestly and explain the options, including load management as an alternative to a full upgrade.

Integration matters just as much as sizing. A battery wired in properly through your consumer unit works seamlessly with your existing circuits; a poorly integrated system can create more electrical complexity than it solves. We handle this as a full certified installation, not a bolt-on.

concerns.q: Is battery storage worth it without solar panels?

deepDive.heading: Why Zone Planning Matters More Than the Alarm Panel Itself
paragraphs: The equipment behind most alarm systems is broadly similar — what actually determines whether a system works well is how the zones are planned. A poorly zoned system either leaves genuine gaps in coverage or triggers so often on false alarms that it gets ignored or switched off, which defeats the purpose entirely.

We plan zones around the property's real layout and how it's actually used — entry points, ground-floor windows, and any areas that need separate arming (like a home office kept active while the rest of the house is set for night mode). That planning, done properly at installation, is what makes the difference between a system that gets used properly and one that becomes background noise.
